title: Are eighty and sixty three co-prime?
description: Eighty and sixty three have no prime in common. The board asks whether a composite number could still divide both. Keeko doubts this and says a composite factor might still be shared.
teaching_notes: One idea: a composite common factor is made of primes, and those primes would sit in both rows of primes. Watch for students who think a composite factor can hide when no prime is shared.

video_script.why: The child sees that if two numbers share no prime, they cannot share a composite factor either, so they are co-prime.
video_script.substitution: the book's own numbers, eighty and sixty three
video_script.anchor: the rows of primes of eighty and sixty three, side by side, with no prime in both
video_script.wrong_answer: a composite factor might still be shared
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko thinks a composite common factor could hide even when no prime is shared.
video_script.payoff_line: Eighty and sixty three are co-prime

final_answer.value: Yes, 80 and 63 are co-prime: a composite common factor would have its prime factors in both factorisations, and no prime is common
final_answer.spoken: eighty and sixty three are co-prime

maths_rules: no prime is in both rows
a composite common factor is a multiplication of primes; each of them divides both numbers, so each sits in both rows
no prime is in both rows, so the only common factor is 1 and 80 and 63 are co-prime
example: 6 = 2 × 3 needs a 2 and a 3 in both numbers, but 63 has no 2 and 80 has no 3

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about eighty and sixty three.
<bookmark mark='rows'/>Eighty is two times two times two times two times five. Sixty three is three times three times seven.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>These two numbers have no prime in common. Can we say they are co-prime?

narration: <bookmark mark='co'/>Two numbers are co-prime when the only number that divides both of them is one.
<bookmark mark='comp'/>A composite number is made by multiplying primes, such as six, which is two times three.

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks a composite factor might still be shared.
<bookmark mark='six'/>Take six, which is two times three. Eighty has a two but no three, and sixty three has a three but no two.
<bookmark mark='strike'/>Six cannot divide both, and the same happens with any composite number here.
